Best of course with others in this case, where as the title suggests, are chained together either in an open chain or closed chain where every member is linked together. I've completed the game with a second player on the easiest difficulty where you can restart from certain places you've reached, and it took a few hours (4 hours 20min funnily enough), though it is easily replayable if you want to play with other people, more people, or different settings such as various difficulties like the Lava Mode. 

There are several areas to progress through, each of which have some unique layout and obstacles. Working together with others is quite fun when you have to work out the best way to get through. Or at some points, you can just dangle on the chain and let the others do the work.

[h2] Chained Together [/h2]

You are looking at a cooperative version of a series of games similar to a "Difficult Game About Climbing" which includes adjustable difficulty and simple checkpoints for those who don't want to suffer, as well as increased difficulty for those who enjoy a challenge. 

The game is both hard and easy at the same time; it's very important to have complete understanding with your team because everything is literally tied to endless quick time events, but for everyone at once - if one person presses at the wrong time, it could mean the end for the whole team. I should mention that even though the game isn't long, there aren't that many 
interesting locations to climb. 

They become much more numerous towards the end, while at the beginning, they're more annoying but overall boring.

The game turned out to be decent, but I'm really sorry that Steam still hasn't added a 'yellow review' option, which I think would be fitting for this game. It's just okay - in a group, you'll probably have fun, but like with any cooperative game, the game itself entertains you very little.

Chained Together turns one of the simplest platforming objectives imaginable into an entertaining exercise in teamwork, precision, and controlled frustration. Developed by Anegar Games and Lab42 and published by Secret Mode, it challenges players to escape from the depths of Hell by climbing an enormous obstacle-filled course. The defining twist is that the participants are physically chained together. Every jump, mistake, and moment of hesitation can therefore affect the entire group, giving the game an identity that extends far beyond being another difficult 3D climbing experience.

The chain is the centerpiece of the gameplay and functions as an actual physics-based object rather than merely representing the connection between players. It can react to structures, wrap around obstacles, become stretched between characters, and influence how a group approaches difficult sections. This creates situations where individual platforming ability is only part of the solution. Players need to consider where their partners are standing, who should move first, and whether a risky jump could compromise everyone else's position. A skilled player cannot simply rush ahead without considering the rest of the team.

Up to four players can participate, and cooperative play is where the concept becomes particularly entertaining. Communication is extremely valuable because groups frequently encounter situations requiring synchronized movement or careful positioning. Successful coordination feels rewarding, while failures can be hilariously destructive. One player missing an apparently easy jump can create a chain reaction that sends everyone tumbling downward. Those moments produce much of the game's humor, especially when a team spends several minutes carefully climbing only to lose progress because of one poorly judged movement.

The game can also be played solo, changing the experience into a more traditional test of platforming skill. Without teammates introducing additional unpredictability, the emphasis shifts toward understanding the course, mastering movement, and improving consistency. Solo play remains challenging and provides a useful way to learn individual sections, but it naturally lacks much of the spontaneous comedy and social tension that make cooperative sessions memorable.

Difficulty options give players some control over how punishing the journey becomes. Beginner Mode includes checkpoints, greatly reducing the consequences of major falls and making the experience more approachable. Normal Mode provides the harsher version of the climb, where losing significant progress becomes a constant possibility. Lava Mode introduces rising lava and forces players to climb under continuous pressure. This variation dramatically changes the pacing because there is far less time to carefully analyze every obstacle. Competitive players can also pursue leaderboard positions and achievements, providing additional motivation to master the more demanding modes.

The obstacle course becomes increasingly elaborate as the ascent continues. Players encounter narrow surfaces, moving platforms, awkward structures, environmental hazards, and jumps that demand increasingly accurate timing. The different areas help provide a sense of progression as the journey moves away from its infernal starting point. Despite the imagery of Hell, Purgatory, and eventual salvation, the tone frequently becomes comedic because physics-based disasters and multiplayer arguments tend to overshadow the darker background elements.

Failure is simultaneously one of the game's greatest strengths and its most obvious source of frustration. The possibility of losing substantial progress makes otherwise ordinary jumps genuinely tense. Reaching a new area after repeated attempts can feel enormously satisfying because success depends primarily on learning and execution rather than upgraded statistics or powerful equipment. However, players who strongly dislike repetition may struggle with this design. Falling because of your own mistake is one thing; watching the entire group collapse because another player mistimed a jump can be considerably more irritating.

Replay value comes from improving climbing efficiency, completing harder modes, earning achievements, and competing for better leaderboard results. Familiarity noticeably changes how the game feels. Sections that initially appear overwhelming eventually become manageable once players understand the movement physics, chain behavior, obstacle patterns, and safest routes. Cooperative groups can develop their own techniques, assigning positions or deciding which player should lead specific sections.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially listed as Unsupported. Players primarily interested in experiencing it on Valve's handheld should keep this limitation in mind rather than assuming that the simple controls automatically guarantee full compatibility. Its design may appear ideal for portable play, but the official Deck classification does not currently provide that assurance.

Visually, the game prioritizes clear environments and recognizable obstacles over elaborate graphical spectacle. This suits the gameplay because players need to judge distances and understand their surroundings quickly. The increasingly unusual environments provide enough visual variety to maintain the feeling of an extended journey. Audio contributes to the infernal atmosphere through environmental sounds and unsettling background details, although conversations and reactions between cooperative players will often become the unofficial soundtrack of a multiplayer session.

The biggest accomplishment of Chained Together is how thoroughly one mechanic influences the entire experience. The chain creates cooperation, competition, comedy, strategy, and frustration without requiring an overly complicated ruleset. The controls are understandable, the objective is immediately clear, and the difficulty emerges naturally from the relationship between movement, obstacles, physics, and teammates. It is easy to understand what must be done but considerably harder to execute it consistently.

Chained Together is ultimately an excellent choice for players who enjoy demanding platformers and cooperative games where mistakes become part of the entertainment. It can be repetitive and occasionally infuriating, and its Steam Deck situation is not as convenient as officially Verified releases. On PC, however, the combination of physics, escalating obstacles, multiple difficulty modes, solo play, and chaotic four-player cooperation creates a focused experience with substantial replay potential. Few things are as satisfying as watching an entire team finally conquer an obstacle that previously sent everyone crashing back down.

Rating: 9/10

I started this game with pure hatred burning in my heart. It’s antilogical, antiphysical, antihuman and aggressively frustrating. Every jump feels like the developers specifically coded gravity just to mock me. It’s less a game and more a carefully engineered rage experiment. And being chained to other people? Let’s just say it’s a quick way to learn how thin the line is between “teammates” and “enemies for life.”

The chain mechanic ensures one clumsy toe-tap turns into a synchronized swan dive to hell. Hours can vanish on a single level, and you’ll swear you’re done, uninstalling in your head at least ten times before you actually quit. Chained Together is not fun. It’s punishment disguised as entertainment.

And yet… somewhere along the way, I started enjoying this f*cking torture. I couldn’t admit it at first, but the game grew on me like a bad rash you eventually learn to scratch in rhythm. Watching my teammates rage, laugh, and actually enjoy the misery somehow made my day. There were even moments I totally enjoyed: like the level at 3400m where we had to memorize the doors (genuinely brilliant), or the spots where you can throw yourself from a ridiculous height and drift all the way down — the freefall feels breathtaking. I deeply recommend that.

Funniest part? My husband soloed the game in about 3.5 hours, while three of us chained idiots took 6 hours. That alone shows how much “extra difficulty” is packed into the multiplayer chaos. And just when you’re on the edge of giving up, the game shifts. The soundtrack turns calming, the scenery becomes peaceful, and you catch yourself wanting more… only for it to end in heaven. Literally. And not.

So here I am: betrayed by my own emotions, recommending a game I swore I hated. Chained Together is rage, joy, absurdity, and strangely unforgettable. I totally hate it.
